Universal Measure for the Impact of Adiabaticity on Quantum Transitions

A matrix-based derivation of target-resolved transfer, separating eigenstate motion, amplitude redistribution, and coherent beating—with phase conventions made explicit.

R. Pant, P. K. Verma, C. Rangi, E. Mondal, M. Bhati, V. Srinivasan, and S. Wüster
Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 126903 (2024)

Section 01What is being measured?

A population can move between two localized states even when the Hamiltonian never changes. In that situation, the instantaneous eigenstates are stationary and their populations are constant; only their relative phases evolve. A different transfer can occur because a populated eigenstate changes its spatial character as nuclei move. Both processes can produce a rising acceptor population, but they have different physical origins.

This paper asks how to distinguish these origins when the dynamics is not cleanly one or the other. Several instantaneous eigenstates may be populated, their amplitudes may change nonadiabatically, and interference may remain important. The proposed quantity is a target-resolved, signed contribution to population transfer, not simply the population of an adiabatic eigenstate and not a universal probability between zero and one.

We derive the published rate expression from the product rule, recast it in matrix form, and test it on exact small-system examples. The discussion also treats phase conventions, amplitude zeros, degeneracies, and extraction from electronic-structure calculations. The published six-page article is the primary source. Its separate publisher supplement was not retrieved; the numerical examples and technical extensions developed here are explicitly tutorial constructions rather than reconstructions of unseen supplementary data.

A useful reading rule. Always specify three things: the Hamiltonian used to define the instantaneous eigenstates, the fixed target projector whose population matters, and the phase convention used while differentiating eigenvectors. Without these, a numerical “adiabaticity measure” is not fully defined.

Primary source: Pant et al., Physical Review Letters 132, 126903 (2024). The central construction is main Eqs. (1), (3), and (5).

Section 02Two bases and one physical state

Let B=(|1⟩,…,|d⟩) be a fixed orthonormal basis. It might label localized excitations, charge-localized electronic states, or angular-momentum states. “Diabatic” in the paper means this time-independent reference basis; it is not a claim that every electronic-structure diabat is unique or exactly time independent.

The Hamiltonian has instantaneous eigenkets |ϕk(t)⟩:

H^(t)|ϕk(t)⟩=Ek(t)|ϕk(t)⟩,⟨ϕj(t)|ϕk(t)⟩=δjk.
(1)

Expand the same state in both bases:

|Ψ(t)⟩=∑ncn(t)|n⟩=∑kc~k(t)|ϕk(t)⟩,Dnk(t)=⟨n|ϕk(t)⟩,cn=∑kDnkc~k.
(2)

The indices have different jobs: n labels a fixed target basis state, while k labels an instantaneous energy eigenstate. They run over the same dimension but are not interchangeable. In the paper, Ek is written Uk, Dnk is written dn(k), and c~k has the same meaning as here.

Section 03The basis transformation as an operator matrix

Introduce a fixed label basis (|k⟩A) for the coefficient space of instantaneous eigenstates. The transformation operator is

U^(t)=∑k|ϕk(t)⟩⟨k|A,[U^]B←A=D,|c⟩B=U^|c~⟩A.
(3)

The column k of D is the fixed-basis representation of eigenket k. Because the eigenvectors are orthonormal, U^†U^=I^, so

|c~⟩A=U^†|c⟩B,U^†H^U^=E^,[E^]A=diag(E1,…,Ed).
(4)

This notation prevents a common numerical mistake: using eigenvectors as rows when the diagonalization routine returns them as columns. A direct implementation should check D†HD, not guess an inverse transformation from the appearance of a plot.

Section 04A target population is an expectation of a fixed projector

Choose one target ket |X⟩ in the fixed basis and define Π^X=|X⟩⟨X|. In the instantaneous eigenbasis the projector is time dependent, even though the physical target is fixed:

Q^X(t)=U^†(t)Π^XU^(t),[Q^X]jk=DXj∗DXk,pX=⟨c~|Q^X|c~⟩=|cX|2.
(5)

For two real eigenvectors related by an angle θ, take

D=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ),[Q^2]=(sin2⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θcos2⁡θ).
(6)

The off-diagonal entries are the interference terms. Ignoring them would replace a coherent pure state by an incoherent mixture and would erase precisely the beating contribution the paper aims to identify.

Section 05Derive the moving-basis Schrödinger equation

Differentiate |c⟩=U^|c~⟩ and substitute the fixed-basis Schrödinger equation. Multiplying on the left by U^† gives

iℏ|c~˙⟩=(E^−iℏA^)|c~⟩,A^=U^†U^˙,Ajk=⟨ϕj|ϕ˙k⟩.
(7)

Differentiate U^†U^=I^:

U^˙†U^+U^†U^˙=0,A^†=−A^.
(8)

Thus −iℏA^ is Hermitian. It is the connection term produced by the moving coordinates, not an extra physical interaction added to the original Hamiltonian. Its off-diagonal entries transfer amplitude between instantaneous eigenstates. Its diagonal entries depend on the eigenvector phases.

Section 06Compute eigenvector derivatives from the Hamiltonian

Differentiate the eigenvalue equation and project with a different eigenbra ⟨ϕj|, j≠k:

⟨ϕj|H^˙|ϕk⟩+Ej⟨ϕj|ϕ˙k⟩=Ek⟨ϕj|ϕ˙k⟩.
(9)

Therefore, for nondegenerate eigenvalues,

Ajk=⟨ϕj|H^˙|ϕk⟩Ek−Ej(j≠k),E˙k=⟨ϕk|H^˙|ϕk⟩.
(10)

These equations are convenient when H^˙ is analytically available. They avoid differencing noisy eigenvectors. They are not valid through an exact degeneracy, where the denominator vanishes and an individual eigenbasis is not uniquely determined. The diagonal Akk must be chosen separately; the parallel-transport convention sets it to zero.

Section 07What the usual adiabatic condition does and does not tell us

A familiar pairwise scale is

ηjk(t)=ℏ|⟨ϕj|H^˙|ϕk⟩||Ek−Ej|2=ℏ|Ajk||Ek−Ej|.
(11)

Small values suggest that eigenstate transitions are weak, subject to conditions on the entire path, gaps, endpoints, duration, and phase accumulation. A local small parameter is not a complete general theorem for arbitrary histories.

More importantly, even perfectly constant eigenstate populations do not determine the fixed-target population when several eigenstates are occupied. They may interfere. The paper's question is therefore different from asking whether η is small or whether one eigenstate remains populated. It asks what portion of a specified transfer comes from changes other than the evolving relative coefficient phases.

Section 08Expand the population and apply the product rule

The target population expands as a double sum:

pX=∑kℓc~ℓ∗c~kDXkDXℓ∗.
(12)

There are four factors in each term. Differentiate each one once while holding the others fixed:

p˙X=∑kℓ[(c~˙ℓ∗c~k+c~ℓ∗c~˙k)DXkDXℓ∗+c~ℓ∗c~k(D˙XkDXℓ∗+DXkD˙Xℓ∗)].
(13)

The second line comes from motion of the eigenvectors. The first line contains changes of both the magnitudes and phases of the instantaneous coefficients. Retaining only the second line is generally insufficient: a changing coordinate frame can generate apparent motion that is canceled by the coefficient changes in the first line.

This is main Eq. (3), with DXk=dX(k).

Section 09Separate coefficient magnitude and phase

Write a nonzero instantaneous coefficient as c~k=akeibk, with ak>0. Its derivative is

c~˙k=eibka˙k+ib˙kc~k.
(14)

The first term is radial motion in the coefficient's complex plane. The second is tangential motion. Define rk=eibka˙k. Without unwrapping any phase,

a˙k=Re(c~k∗c~˙k)|c~k|,rk=Re(c~k∗c~˙k)|c~k|2c~k,b˙k=Im(c~k∗c~˙k)|c~k|2.
(15)

These formulas follow by multiplying the derivative by c~k∗=ake−ibk: the real part is aka˙k, and the imaginary part is ak2b˙k. They are valid only away from coefficient zeros; the zero case is treated below rather than hidden by an arbitrary denominator replacement.

Section 10Derive the paper's central rate in a compact form

In the differentiated population, retain the radial coefficient terms and all eigenvector-motion terms, and omit the explicit b˙k terms. Define a fixed-basis ket

|ξ⟩B=U^˙|c~⟩A+U^|r⟩A.
(16)

The resulting target rate is

fX(t)=2Re[cX∗(t)ξX(t)]=2Re⟨Ψ|Π^X|ξ⟩.
(17)

Expand cX∗=∑ℓDXℓ∗c~ℓ∗ and add the complex conjugate. One obtains

fX=∑kℓ[(rℓ∗c~k+c~ℓ∗rk)DXkDXℓ∗+c~ℓ∗c~k(D˙XkDXℓ∗+DXkD˙Xℓ∗)].
(18)

Substituting rk=a˙keibk recovers main Eq. (5). The compact form costs matrix–ket products rather than an explicit four-index implementation. It also makes the reality of fX transparent.

Source: main Eq. (5). The compact ket representation is derived here from that expression.

Section 11The phase contribution and an exact bookkeeping identity

Let B^ph=diag(b˙1,…,b˙d) in instantaneous coefficient space. The omitted contribution is

bXrate=2Re[cX∗(U^iB^ph|c~⟩)X],p˙X=fX+bXrate.
(19)

The symbol bXrate is a target rate; it must not be confused with the phase bk of an eigenstate coefficient. To avoid dividing by small coefficients twice, a numerical implementation can compute U^(|c~˙⟩−|r⟩) for this phase term.

Integrating both contributions gives

TX(t)=∫0tfX(s)ds,BX(t)=∫0tbXrate(s)ds,pX(t)−pX(0)=TX(t)+BX(t).
(20)

This is an excellent numerical check. It is not a claim that the two integrals are separately probabilities, positive, or independent counterfactual experiments.

Section 12Conservation and target subspaces

Sum over a complete fixed basis. Unitarity makes the eigenvector contribution purely imaginary, and normalization makes the radial contribution sum to zero:

∑XfX=2Re[⟨c~|A^|c~⟩+⟨c~|r⟩]=2∑kaka˙k=ddt∑kak2=0.
(21)

The phase rates also sum to zero. Therefore ∑XTX=0 when all integrals start at zero: positive contributions to one target are balanced by negative contributions elsewhere.

For a target subspace, use a fixed projector Π^S=∑X∈S|X⟩⟨X|. Then fS=∑X∈SfX. This is invariant under a change of orthonormal basis within the same fixed target subspace, because only its projector appears. Changing the physical target projector is a different question, not a coordinate change.

Section 13Why T is not automatically between zero and one

The integral TX is signed. It can increase when state following helps a target gain population and decrease when it removes population from the target. Interference can compensate for these changes through BX. Consequently, the algebra supplies no general interval 0≤TX≤1.

For an initially empty target and an almost purely adiabatic transfer, TX≃pX is a useful limiting interpretation. For a target with nonzero initial population, the corresponding comparison is to pX(t)−pX(0), not to pX(t) alone. Dividing by a very small final population can produce an unstable or very large ratio; it should not be reported as a meaningful “percentage” without context.

The measure is a decomposition along the realized dynamics. It does not independently simulate what would have happened if the nuclei had stopped moving or if the Hamiltonian had been frozen. Those are additional counterfactual simulations with different trajectories.

Section 14Constant two-state Hamiltonian: transfer without state following

In the fixed basis (|1⟩,|2⟩), consider

[H^]=(Δ/2JJ−Δ/2),E=J2+Δ2/4,H^2=E2I^.
(22)

Use the power series and separate even and odd terms:

e−iH^t/ℏ=cos⁡(Et/ℏ)I^−isin⁡(Et/ℏ)H^E.
(23)

Starting from |1⟩,

|Ψ(t)⟩=[cos⁡(Et/ℏ)−iΔ2Esin⁡(Et/ℏ)]|1⟩−iJEsin⁡(Et/ℏ)|2⟩,p2(t)=J2E2sin2⁡(Et/ℏ).
(24)

The instantaneous eigenvectors are constant, and each eigenstate coefficient changes only by its energy phase. Thus U^˙=0, |r⟩=0, and f2=T2=0. For Δ=2, J=1, and ℏ=1, the target population is 12sin2⁡(2t), while its adiabatic contribution vanishes exactly.

Section 15Constant three-state chain: perfect transfer can still be beating

A three-state example avoids relying only on a qubit. Set all site energies to zero and nearest-neighbor couplings to J:

[H^]=(0J0J0J0J0),[U^]=(1/21/21/21/20−1/21/2−1/21/2),[E^]=diag(2J,0,−2J).
(25)

For |Ψ(0)⟩=|1⟩, the eigenbasis coefficient ket is (1/2,1/2,1/2)T. Reconstructing the third-site amplitude gives

c3(t)=12[cos⁡(2Jt/ℏ)−1],p3(t)=sin4⁡(Jt2ℏ),T3(t)=0.
(26)

At the first maximum, all population reaches site 3. A transfer efficiency of one therefore does not imply that the mechanism was adiabatic following. This resonant-chain example is an analytic teaching case; the first figure of the paper also explores a three-state system with unequal site energies.

Section 16A rotating two-state Hamiltonian with an exact solution

Let U^(t) be the real rotation by θ(t)=ωrt, and let E^=Eσ^z. Define the physical Hamiltonian H^(t)=U^(t)E^U^†(t). Its gap 2E is fixed while its eigenvectors rotate.

A^=(0−ωrωr0)=−iωrσ^y,H^rot=Eσ^z−ℏωrσ^y.
(27)

The rotating-frame Hamiltonian is constant. Therefore the exact physical solution is

|Ψ(t)⟩=U^(t)e−i(Eσ^z−ℏωrσ^y)t/ℏ|1⟩.
(28)

This provides a clean test of both propagation and the moving-basis connection. When ℏωr/(2E)≪1, the second rotating-frame coefficient remains small and the population approximately follows p2≃sin2⁡θ. Nevertheless, calculate T2 from the exact solution rather than inferring it from that small leakage alone: switching on a nonzero angular velocity at the initial time produces a small rapidly changing eigenbasis component, and the measure contains phase derivatives as well as amplitudes. At finite rotation speed, simply prescribing a rotating eigenket would not solve the original Schrödinger equation. The following passage example uses a rotation speed that vanishes at both endpoints to avoid that abrupt onset.

Section 17An ideal three-state passage and its dark eigenket

For a different teaching case, make the two endpoint energies equal and allow an intermediate detuning Δ:

[H^(t)]=(0J12(t)0J12(t)ΔJ23(t)0J23(t)0).
(29)

Define V=J122+J232 and tan⁡θ=J12/J23. Direct multiplication proves that

|D⟩=cos⁡θ|1⟩−sin⁡θ|3⟩,H^|D⟩=0.
(30)

The orthogonal endpoint combination |B⟩=sin⁡θ|1⟩+cos⁡θ|3⟩ couples to |2⟩. In the ordered basis (|D⟩,|B⟩,|2⟩),

[H^]=(00000V0VΔ),E±=Δ±Δ2+4V22.
(31)

Turning on J23 first and then J12 rotates the dark ket from |1⟩ to −|3⟩. The minus sign is a phase, not a negative population. This exactly dark eigenstate requires equal endpoint energies; it must not be assumed for every nondegenerate trimer in the paper.

Section 18Derive the target rate in the adiabatic passage limit

The derivative of the dark ket is |D˙⟩=−θ˙|B⟩. Thus the moving-basis coupling between dark and bright directions is set by θ˙. The nearest gap to the dark state is

Δmin=Δ2+4V2−|Δ|2,ℏ|θ˙|≪Δminas a useful passage scale.
(32)

In the ideal adiabatic limit, only the dark eigenstate is occupied, its coefficient magnitude stays constant, and its target probability is sin2⁡θ. Consequently,

f3(t)≃2sin⁡θcos⁡θθ˙,T3(t)≃sin2⁡θ(t)−sin2⁡θ(0).
(33)

The browser demonstration below propagates the actual three-state Schrödinger equation and evaluates the measure from that solution. It does not substitute this limiting expression and then label the result a finite-speed simulation. The limiting curve is used only as a reference.

Section 19Why amplitude derivatives must not be omitted

Consider an abrupt eigenbasis rotation over a time so short that the physical state hardly changes. At leading order |c˙⟩≃0, so the two moving-coordinate terms obey

U^˙|c~⟩+U^|c~˙⟩≃0,|c~˙⟩≃−A^|c~⟩.
(34)

Take a real two-component physical ket (|1⟩+|2⟩)/2, away from zeros of the instantaneous coefficients. A rotation with angular speed ωr gives an eigenvector-only contribution f2vectors=ωr, even though the physical target population remains 1/2. The radial coefficient term contributes −ωr, canceling it.

This is a kinematic fast-change limit that explains the first line of main Eq. (5). Keeping only D˙ mistakes changing coordinates for actual transfer. The full measure remains a decomposition of the realized dynamics, not a test that every retained contribution is independently an adiabatic transition in the theorem's strict sense.

Section 20Phase conventions: a subtle but essential part of the definition

An eigensolver may multiply each eigenket by an arbitrary phase. A constant phase is harmless if all coefficients are transformed consistently. A time-dependent phase changes the derivative split. Let

|ϕk′⟩=eiχk(t)|ϕk⟩,c~k′=e−iχk(t)c~k,Dnk′=eiχk(t)Dnk.
(35)

The physical products Dnkc~k and all target populations are unchanged. However, differentiating D′ adds a term to the literal radial-plus-eigenvector rate:

fX′=fX+2Re[cX∗∑kiχ˙kDXkc~k].
(36)

The phase contribution changes by the opposite amount, so p˙X remains invariant. The two pieces separately require a convention. For the real Hamiltonians in the paper's model examples, smooth real eigenvectors with consistent signs provide a natural local convention. For complex Hamiltonians, we use parallel transport, ⟨ϕk|ϕ˙k⟩=0, along the time path. This is an explicit implementation convention, not an assertion that the literal split is invariant under arbitrary independently time-dependent eigenvector phases.

Section 21A phase-covariant way to evaluate the chosen convention

Define the diagonal part A^diag=diag(A11,…,Add) and the covariant eigenvector derivative

∇tU^=U^˙−U^A^diag.
(37)

Under rephasing, ∇tU^ acquires only the same column phases as U^; the extra χ˙k terms cancel. The convention-fixed rate can therefore be evaluated as

fX∥=2Re[cX∗((∇tU^)|c~⟩+U^|r⟩)X].
(38)

In a parallel-transport gauge this equals the published expression directly. This covariant evaluation is a tutorial implementation refinement: it makes the selected gauge prescription reproducible even when instantaneous eigenvectors arrive with arbitrary phases. The teaching code uses the off-diagonal derivative-coupling formula with diagonal connection set to zero, which implements this convention for nondegenerate eigenvalues.

It does not remove the additional freedom to mix eigenvectors inside an exactly degenerate subspace. Phase freedom and degenerate-subspace rotations are different issues.

Section 22Coefficient zeros and a practical local limit

At c~k=0, its phase is undefined and the ratio defining rk is formally singular. Adding a fixed tiny number to every denominator changes the measure near zeros and can conceal errors.

For an isolated smooth simple zero, locally c~k(t)≃z1(t−t0). The radial derivative approached from either side satisfies rk→z1=c~˙k(t0). This gives a natural continuation for this case. A coefficient that stays identically zero also has zero derivative.

The script uses the local continuation rk=c~˙k below a small amplitude threshold and reports/checks threshold sensitivity in its tests. This is a numerical convention for smooth isolated zeros, not a general theorem about arbitrarily noisy or discontinuous trajectories. The integrated quantity should converge when the timestep and threshold are reduced; unresolved spikes are a warning, not interesting physics by default.

Section 23Eigenvector tracking for saved trajectories

When H^˙ is unavailable, diagonalize each saved Hamiltonian and compare neighboring eigenvectors. First match the columns by overlap, taking care with very small gaps. Then align the phase of each matched new column so that its overlap with the previous column is real and positive:

sk=⟨ϕk(tj)|ϕk(tj+1)⟩,|ϕk(tj+1)⟩←e−iarg⁡sk|ϕk(tj+1)⟩.
(39)

Only after this step should one finite-difference eigenvectors and transformed coefficients. A coarse time step can make maximum-overlap matching follow the wrong branch across an avoided crossing. Energy ordering is appropriate for well-resolved nondegenerate adiabatic branches; overlap matching detects accidental reordering, but cannot replace time resolution.

If |sk| is small, reduce the saved interval or treat a near-degenerate block together. Report the orthogonality error, minimum energy gap, and the size of the frame increment. “The eigenvectors looked smooth” is not a quantitative convergence check.

Section 24Exact degeneracies and what subspace tracking can establish

Within an exactly degenerate eigenspace, any unitary mixture of its eigenvectors is another equally valid eigenbasis. The individual magnitudes |c~k| and their radial derivatives then depend on that internal choice. The nondegenerate construction cannot be made unique merely by flipping signs or sorting energies.

One can track the spectral projector of a degenerate block and transport an orthonormal frame by overlap or a polar decomposition. This yields a smooth convention, but a claim of invariance under all internal unitary rotations requires a block-level definition, not the unmodified scalar coefficient formula. The teaching implementation deliberately stops if an exact or unresolved degeneracy is encountered instead of returning a deceptively precise number.

A related point is that H^(t) itself must be specified. If a counterdiabatic control term is physically applied, the instantaneous eigenstates of the full Hamiltonian need not coincide with those of the reference Hamiltonian that the control was designed to follow. A measure relative to the reference Hamiltonian and one relative to the full Hamiltonian answer different questions.

Section 25A four-state matrix example with more than one target

Suppose a donor pair and an acceptor pair form a four-state system. In (|1⟩,|2⟩,|3⟩,|4⟩), one possible Hamiltonian is

[H^(t)]=(ϵ1JDK(t)0JDϵ20K(t)K(t)0ϵ3JA0K(t)JAϵ4),[Π^A]=diag(0,0,1,1).
(40)

A single acceptor-site target uses Π^3; the complete acceptor region uses Π^A. Compute |ξ⟩ once. Then

f3=2Re(c3∗ξ3),f4=2Re(c4∗ξ4),fA=f3+f4.
(41)

A rotation of the basis within the span of (|3⟩,|4⟩) may redistribute f3 and f4, but it leaves fA unchanged when the projector is the same. This is useful for molecular fragments or spatial regions where an individual basis function is not the observable of interest. It also shows why a target-resolved measure need not be restricted to a single atom or molecule.

Section 26What the molecular-aggregate examples establish

The paper's moving-aggregate Hamiltonian contains localized excitations with site energies and distance-dependent couplings. The characteristic off-diagonal form is

H^agg(t)=∑nϵn|n⟩⟨n|+∑n≠mμ2|Xn(t)−Xm(t)|3|n⟩⟨m|.
(42)

Here Xn(t) is a scalar coordinate along the aggregate; an ensemble of coordinates can be represented as the classical configuration ket |X(t)⟩. Distances change the electronic matrix elements, so nuclear motion changes the eigenvectors. The paper compares cases in which transfer is dominated by beating, by near-adiabatic following, or by mixtures involving nonadiabatic events.

The important methodological point is not that every moving molecule produces adiabatic transport. It is that TX can distinguish which part of a complicated time trace contributes to arrival at a chosen target and which part is largely phase beating. The signed integral can decrease when an earlier adiabatic contribution is removed. A target population alone cannot make that distinction.

Source: main Fig. 2 and its discussion. The teaching code below uses transparent small matrices, not the unpublished trajectory data underlying that figure.

Section 27The TCNE charge-transfer example and the required inputs

The paper then applies the construction to a tetracyanoethylene trimer carrying an additional electron. It uses electronic-structure calculations to obtain approximate adiabatic states, charge-localized reference states, and their overlaps. The middle molecule is moved between the two outer molecules along an intentionally fast prescribed path; this is a proof-of-principle setting, not a claim that the imposed motion is a typical thermal molecular trajectory.

The two inputs to the rate expression remain the same:

Dnk(t)=⟨n|ϕk(t)⟩,|c~(t)⟩,together with their time dependence.
(43)

The reported final ratio for the illustrated target is T3(tf)/|c3(tf)|2≃0.8. It refers to that calculation and its choices of states and motion, not a universal fraction for charge transfer in TCNE. Reproducing the value requires the original electronic-structure inputs and trajectory; it cannot be inferred from a generic three-state Hamiltonian.

Source: main Fig. 3 and charge-transfer discussion. The original paper uses the author name “E. Mondal”; that bibliographic spelling is preserved in the citation.

Section 28How determinant overlaps enter a many-electron representation

For two normalized Slater determinants constructed from occupied spin orbitals, the overlap is a determinant of the one-electron overlap matrix:

⟨ΦA|ΦB⟩=detS^AB,SijAB=⟨χiA|χjB⟩.
(44)

An approximate excited state written as a sum of singly excited determinants has overlap

|ϕk⟩≃∑iaCia(k)|Φia⟩,Dnk≃∑iaCia(k)⟨Φn|Φia⟩.
(45)

This demonstrates the algebra behind constructing the necessary state-overlap matrix. It does not assert that a TDDFT response vector is an exact many-electron wavefunction or that every implementation uses identical spin adaptation, normalization, or excitation amplitudes. Those choices must be specified in a reproducible electronic-structure calculation.

The paper describes a route using DFT/TDDFT and constrained DFT reference states, followed by propagation of adiabatic coefficients with derivative couplings. The measure itself does not repair errors in those approximate states or couplings; it analyzes the dynamics supplied to it.

Section 29Nonorthogonal or moving reference states require extra care

Charge-localized reference states obtained independently may not be orthogonal. With overlap matrix S^, the norm is ⟨c|S^|c⟩, not ∑n|cn|2, and the spectral problem is generalized:

H^|dk⟩=EkS^|dk⟩,H^orth=S^−1/2H^S^−1/2,|corth⟩=S^1/2|c⟩.
(46)

For a fixed positive-definite S^, symmetric orthogonalization supplies an orthonormal coordinate representation. It also changes the interpretation of individual coefficients; define the physical charge or target projector in that representation rather than treating every transformed coefficient as a uniquely localized charge.

If the reference basis itself moves with the nuclei, its derivatives add a connection to the fixed-reference derivation. One must include this motion or map all states into a consistent reference representation. Directly inserting raw nonorthogonal, moving-basis coefficients into the paper's orthonormal fixed-basis formula is not justified. This section states a general implementation requirement; it does not claim that a particular extra approximation was used in the published TCNE calculation.

Section 30Why a mixed-state extension is not automatic

For a density operator, the target population is pX=Tr(Π^Xρ^). In the instantaneous basis,

ρ^~=U^†ρ^U^,ρ^~˙=−iℏ[E^,ρ^~]−[A^,ρ^~]+D^ρ^~
(47)

when the physical dynamics includes a dissipator D^. The population derivative follows by the product rule with Q^X, but the pure-state radial operation contains ratios involving individual amplitudes. It is not simply a linear superoperator acting on ρ^.

A trajectory average of pure-state measures can be meaningful for a specified physical trajectory ensemble. It should not be claimed to define an ensemble-decomposition-independent mixed-state measure without proof. For open-system applications, specify whether the aim is to separate coherent phase beating, basis motion, bath-induced population transfer, or a chosen unraveling of the bath dynamics.

Section 31Implementation algorithm and error checks

Propagate the physical ket in a fixed basis. At each saved time, obtain H^, its eigenvectors, and either H^˙ or a sufficiently resolved neighboring set of eigenvectors. Transform the state into the instantaneous basis. In the analytic-derivative route, compute the off-diagonal connection using energy gaps and set its diagonal to zero. Then compute |c~˙⟩=(−iE^/ℏ−A^)|c~⟩, the radial ket, and |ξ⟩.

Save pX, fX, and the phase rate at the same times, and integrate with a controlled quadrature rule. Converge the propagation timestep, output interval, integration quadrature, and amplitude threshold separately. A fourth-order propagation method does not make a subsequent coarse trapezoidal integral fourth order.

Check norm conservation, eigenvector orthogonality, ∑XfX=0, and the integrated identity pX−pX(0)=TX+BX. Compare the analytic-connection implementation against smooth finite differences for a small model. Repeat with arbitrary constant eigenvector phases: a convention-consistent result should not change. A random sign flip at every time is a deliberately broken finite-difference gauge, not a physical perturbation.

Section 32Interactive three-state passage

The following calculation uses the resonant-endpoint Hamiltonian derived above, with ℏ=1, J12=Vsin⁡θ(t), and J23=Vcos⁡θ(t). We choose a smooth turn-on and turn-off:

θ(t)=π4[1−cos⁡(πttf)],θ˙(t)=π24tfsin⁡(πttf).
(48)

The norm J122+J232=V is constant, and the eigenvector rotation speed vanishes at both endpoints. This is a tutorial protocol, distinct from the squared-pulse, nondegenerate example in the paper. With V=1, Δ=0, tf=30, and 4000 integration intervals, the accompanying reference implementation gives approximately p3=0.999817, T3=0.976878, and B3=0.022939. These are newly calculated teaching values, not published data. Their sum verifies the population-change identity; it does not make either contribution a separate probability.

The state starts in |1⟩. The displayed result is a numerical Schrödinger propagation and the parallel-gauge form of the published measure, not the ideal limiting curve. Increase the step count to check the integral residual and endpoint stability.

Section 33Exercises with worked solutions

1. Which coefficients are changed by a basis transformation?

The physical ket remains fixed. If columns of D are instantaneous eigenvectors, |c⟩=D|c~⟩ and |c~⟩=D†|c⟩. Populations of different physical projectors may differ; the norm and any consistently transformed observable do not.

2. Prove that the connection is anti-Hermitian.

Differentiate D†D=I to obtain D˙†D+D†D˙=0. The first term is the adjoint of the second, so A†=−A. The moving-frame correction −iℏA is consequently Hermitian.

3. Derive the off-diagonal derivative coupling.

Differentiate H^|ϕk⟩=Ek|ϕk⟩, multiply by ⟨ϕj| for j≠k, and use orthogonality. Rearrangement gives Ajk=⟨ϕj|H^˙|ϕk⟩/(Ek−Ej). It cannot be applied at a zero gap.

4. Show that the target projector contains interference.

For target 2 in the rotated two-state basis, the off-diagonal projector element is sin⁡θcos⁡θ. Therefore its population includes 2sin⁡θcos⁡θRe(c~1∗c~2). Removing this term would change the state description to an incoherent mixture.

5. Evaluate T for the constant Hamiltonian with Δ = 2 and J = 1.

The eigenvectors are constant and the eigenstate coefficient magnitudes do not change. Both terms in |ξ⟩ vanish, so T2=0, even though p2=12sin2⁡(2t) for ℏ=1.

6. When does the resonant three-state chain first transfer completely?

The population is p3=sin4⁡[Jt/(2ℏ)]. Its first maximum occurs at t=πℏ/(2J). The Hamiltonian is constant, so the adiabatic contribution is still zero at that perfect-transfer time.

7. Verify the passage dark ket explicitly.

Acting on cos⁡θ|1⟩−sin⁡θ|3⟩ produces only a middle-state amplitude J12cos⁡θ−J23sin⁡θ. It vanishes when tan⁡θ=J12/J23. Equal endpoint energies are required for the stated zero-energy eigenket.

8. Obtain the ideal target rate during dark-state passage.

The target population is sin2⁡θ. Its derivative is 2sin⁡θcos⁡θθ˙. A single occupied adiabatic coefficient has constant magnitude, and its phase drops from this population, so the derivative equals the limiting f3.

9. What changes if the target initially has population?

The exact integrated relation is ΔpX=TX+BX. Pure state following gives TX=pX(t)−pX(0). Comparing to the final population without subtracting the initial value would incorrectly count population that never arrived during the interval.

10. Why is the eigenvector-only formula unsafe in a sudden change?

The physical state can remain almost fixed while the eigenbasis rotates rapidly. The apparent contribution from D˙ is then canceled by changing coefficient magnitudes. The uniform real two-state ket example gives +ωr and −ωr for the two contributions to target 2.

11. Is the split invariant under arbitrary time-dependent eigenvector phases?

Not literally. Rephasing adds 2Re[cX∗∑kiχ˙kDXkc~k] to fX, and subtracts it from the phase rate. Fix a parallel-transport convention, or use the equivalent covariant derivative given on this page.

12. How do you remove an arbitrary sign flip between neighboring eigenvectors?

Compute their overlap s. Multiply the new vector by e−iarg⁡s, which is simply a sign change for real eigenvectors. This makes the overlap positive real. A very small overlap indicates inadequate time resolution or a need for subspace tracking.

13. What is the radial term at a simple coefficient zero?

For c~(t)=z1(t−t0)+⋯, the radial contribution approached from either side tends to z1. Assigning that local limit avoids a literal division by zero. The threshold and time resolution must still be checked, especially for noisy or multiple zeros.

14. Can the sum of all target contributions be positive?

For a complete orthonormal set of fixed targets and normalized unitary dynamics, no: ∑XfX=0, so ∑XTX=0. Summing absolute values defines a different activity-like quantity and counts reversible contributions rather than net population transfer.

15. Why is a nonorthogonal charge basis not handled by |c_n|²?

The norm is ⟨c|S|c⟩, including overlap cross terms. One must orthogonalize or define physical projectors with the metric included. Raw expansion coefficients in a nonorthogonal basis are not a set of mutually exclusive population probabilities.

16. Is a computed T₃/p₃ of 0.8 a universal result?

No. It is the reported ratio for the paper's particular TCNE illustration. Different initial states, reference projectors, nuclear paths, electronic-structure approximations, or target populations can change the value. A nearly empty target also makes the ratio numerically unstable.

Section 34Download the implementation and test it

Download the NumPy teaching script. It implements fixed-basis propagation, analytic nondegenerate derivative couplings, the parallel-gauge measure, the radial continuation near simple zeros, and integrated conservation checks. Tests include constant two- and three-state Hamiltonians, the exactly solvable rotating frame, a real three-state passage, and phase-covariance checks.

python adiabaticity_measure_teaching.py --test
python adiabaticity_measure_teaching.py --demo --output adiabaticity_demo.csv

All propagation examples use consistent dimensionless units with ℏ=1. The demo is not an electronic-structure reproduction of the TCNE example. A real application should supply its own physical Hamiltonian, state trajectory, and target definition, and should report convergence of the derived measure as carefully as convergence of the populations.

Primary citation: R. Pant, P. K. Verma, C. Rangi, E. Mondal, M. Bhati, V. Srinivasan, and S. Wüster, “Universal Measure for the Impact of Adiabaticity on Quantum Transitions,” Physical Review Letters 132, 126903 (2024), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.126903. The phase-covariant implementation, extra examples, and numerical safeguards above are tutorial derivations with their assumptions stated, not separate claims of new published results.
